```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(openintro)
library(patchwork)
options(scipen = 999)

crimson <- "#A51C30"
navy <- "#3B4B61"
pink <- "#F6D5DA"

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 22))

circle_path <- function(cx, cy = 0, r = 1) {
  tibble(t = seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200), x = cx + r * cos(t), y = cy + r * sin(t))
}

# ---- Die Venn diagram: A = even, B = odd, C = prime ----------------------
# A and B do not overlap; C overlaps both.
# `region(a, b, c)` is TRUE where the diagram is shaded.
die_venn <- function(region = function(a, b, c) FALSE, title = NULL, fill = crimson,
                     text_col = "white") {
  inA <- function(x, y) (x + 1.1)^2 + y^2 <= 0.9^2
  inB <- function(x, y) (x - 1.1)^2 + y^2 <= 0.9^2
  inC <- function(x, y) x^2 + (y + 0.1)^2 <= 0.85^2
  grid <- expand_grid(x = seq(-2.4, 2.4, length.out = 400),
                      y = seq(-1.5, 1.5, length.out = 250)) |>
    mutate(shade = region(inA(x, y), inB(x, y), inC(x, y)))
  nums <- tibble(x = c(-1.5, -1.5, -0.5, 0.48, 0.48, 1.6),
                 y = c(0.3, -0.3, -0.05, 0.22, -0.32, 0),
                 label = c("4", "6", "2", "3", "5", "1")) |>
    mutate(shaded = region(inA(x, y), inB(x, y), inC(x, y)))
  p <- ggplot() +
    geom_raster(data = grid, aes(x, y, fill = shade), show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "white", `TRUE` = fill)) +
    geom_path(data = circle_path(-1.1, 0, 0.9), aes(x, y), linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_path(data = circle_path(1.1, 0, 0.9), aes(x, y), linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_path(data = circle_path(0, -0.1, 0.85), aes(x, y), linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_text(data = nums, aes(x, y, label = label, color = shaded), size = 10, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "black", `TRUE` = text_col)) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = -2.4, xmax = 2.4, ymin = -1.5, ymax = 1.5,
             fill = NA, color = "black", linewidth = 1.2) +
    annotate("text", x = c(-1.75, 1.75, 0), y = c(1.15, 1.15, -1.22),
             label = c("A", "B", "C"), size = 10, fontface = "bold") +
    annotate("text", x = -2.2, y = 1.3, label = "S", size = 9, fontface = "italic") +
    coord_equal() + theme_void()
  if (!is.null(title)) {
    p <- p + labs(title = title) + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 26))
  }
  p
}

# ---- Two-event Venn diagram (used with the GSS data) ----------------------
venn2 <- function(region = function(a, b) FALSE, labels = c("B", "C"),
                  counts = NULL, title = NULL) {
  in1 <- function(x, y) (x + 0.6)^2 + y^2 <= 1
  in2 <- function(x, y) (x - 0.6)^2 + y^2 <= 1
  grid <- expand_grid(x = seq(-2.4, 2.4, length.out = 400),
                      y = seq(-1.6, 1.6, length.out = 270)) |>
    mutate(shade = region(in1(x, y), in2(x, y)))
  p <- ggplot() +
    geom_raster(data = grid, aes(x, y, fill = shade), show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "white", `TRUE` = crimson)) +
    geom_path(data = circle_path(-0.6), aes(x, y), linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_path(data = circle_path(0.6), aes(x, y), linewidth = 1.2) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = -2.4, xmax = 2.4, ymin = -1.6, ymax = 1.6,
             fill = NA, color = "black", linewidth = 1.2) +
    annotate("text", x = c(-1.55, 1.55), y = 1.2, label = labels, size = 10, fontface = "bold") +
    annotate("text", x = -2.15, y = 1.35, label = "S", size = 9, fontface = "italic") +
    coord_equal() + theme_void()
  if (!is.null(counts)) {
    pos <- tibble(x = c(-1.1, 0, 1.1, 1.85), y = c(0, 0, 0, -1.2), label = counts) |>
      mutate(shaded = region(in1(x, y), in2(x, y)))
    p <- p + geom_text(data = pos, aes(x, y, label = label, color = shaded),
                       size = 8, show.legend = FALSE) +
      scale_color_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "black", `TRUE` = "white"))
  }
  if (!is.null(title)) {
    p <- p + labs(title = title) + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 26))
  }
  p
}

# ---- Generic three-event Venn diagram (practice) ----------------------------
venn3 <- function(region = function(a, b, c) FALSE, fill = crimson, title = NULL) {
  grid <- expand_grid(x = seq(-2.4, 2.4, length.out = 400),
                      y = seq(-1.9, 1.7, length.out = 300)) |>
    mutate(inA = (x + 0.55)^2 + (y - 0.35)^2 <= 1,
           inB = (x - 0.55)^2 + (y - 0.35)^2 <= 1,
           inC = x^2 + (y + 0.55)^2 <= 1,
           shade = region(inA, inB, inC))
  p <- ggplot() +
    geom_raster(data = grid, aes(x, y, fill = shade), show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "white", `TRUE` = fill)) +
    geom_path(data = circle_path(-0.55, 0.35), aes(x, y), linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_path(data = circle_path(0.55, 0.35), aes(x, y), linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_path(data = circle_path(0, -0.55), aes(x, y), linewidth = 1.2) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = -2.4, xmax = 2.4, ymin = -1.9, ymax = 1.7,
             fill = NA, color = "black", linewidth = 1.2) +
    annotate("text", x = c(-1.55, 1.55, 1.2), y = c(1.35, 1.35, -1.45),
             label = c("A", "B", "C"), size = 10, fontface = "bold") +
    annotate("text", x = -2.15, y = 1.45, label = "S", size = 9, fontface = "italic") +
    coord_equal() + theme_void()
  if (!is.null(title)) {
    p <- p + labs(title = title) + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 22))
  }
  p
}

# ---- Die faces and coins ---------------------------------------------------
pip_layout <- list(
  `1` = list(c(0, 0)),
  `2` = list(c(-1, 1), c(1, -1)),
  `3` = list(c(-1, 1), c(0, 0), c(1, -1)),
  `4` = list(c(-1, 1), c(1, 1), c(-1, -1), c(1, -1)),
  `5` = list(c(-1, 1), c(1, 1), c(0, 0), c(-1, -1), c(1, -1)),
  `6` = list(c(-1, 1), c(1, 1), c(-1, 0), c(1, 0), c(-1, -1), c(1, -1))
)
dice_faces <- function(highlight = integer(0)) {
  faces <- tibble(face = 1:6, cx = (1:6) * 3) |> mutate(hl = face %in% highlight)
  pips <- map_dfr(1:6, \(f) map_dfr(pip_layout[[f]], \(p) tibble(face = f, dx = p[1], dy = p[2]))) |>
    left_join(faces, by = "face") |>
    mutate(x = cx + 0.65 * dx, y = 0.65 * dy)
  ggplot() +
    geom_tile(data = faces, aes(cx, 0, fill = hl), width = 2.4, height = 2.4,
              color = "black", linewidth = 1.2, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "white", `TRUE` = crimson)) +
    geom_point(data = pips, aes(x, y, color = hl), size = 5, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "black", `TRUE` = "white")) +
    annotate("text", x = faces$cx, y = -1.8, label = 1:6, size = 8) +
    coord_equal(ylim = c(-2.4, 1.4)) + theme_void()
}
coin_flips <- function(outcomes) {
  tibble(label = outcomes, i = seq_along(outcomes)) |>
    mutate(pair = ceiling(i / 2), pos = (i - 1) %% 2, x = pair * 3.2 + pos * 1.1) |>
    ggplot(aes(x, 0)) +
    geom_point(size = 22, shape = 21, fill = "#E8C468", color = "#8A6A12", stroke = 2) +
    geom_text(aes(label = label), size = 10, fontface = "bold") +
    coord_equal(xlim = c(2.4, ceiling(length(outcomes) / 2) * 3.2 + 1.9), ylim = c(-0.8, 0.8)) +
    theme_void()
}
```

## Random process

In random processes there is more than one possible outcome and the deterministic prediction of the outcome is difficult.

- e.g. flip of a coin
- e.g. roll of a die

## Sample space

**Sample space** is the set of all possible outcomes of a random process.

. . .

::: {.stat-callout .example}
**Examples**

In a single roll of a die:

$S = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$

In flipping a single coin twice:

$S = \{HH, TT, HT, TH\}$
:::

## Sample space

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 1.6
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "The six faces of a die, showing 1 through 6 pips, with the numbers 1 to 6 written underneath."
dice_faces()
```

$S = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 1.4
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Four pairs of gold coins showing the four possible results of two coin flips: H H, T T, H T, and T H."
coin_flips(c("H", "H", "T", "T", "H", "T", "T", "H"))
```

$S = \{HH, TT, HT, TH\}$

## Event {.smaller}

An __event__ is a subset of the sample space.

::: {.stat-callout .example}
**Examples**

Let A represent the event that a single roll die results in an *even* number.

$A = \{2, 4, 6\}$

Let B represent the event that a single roll die results in an *odd* number.

$B = \{1, 3, 5\}$

Let C represent the event that a single roll die results in a *prime* number.

$C = \{2, 3, 5\}$
:::

## Venn diagram

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Venn diagram for a single roll of a die. A rectangle labeled S contains three circles. Circle A, even, holds 4, 6, and 2. Circle B, odd, holds 1, 3, and 5. A and B do not overlap. Circle C, prime, drawn with a dashed line, sits in the middle and overlaps both: it contains 2 from A and 3 and 5 from B."
die_venn()
```

$A$ = even, $B$ = odd, $C$ = prime

## Complement of an event

**Definition** Complement of an event is the set of all outcomes in the sample space that are not in the event itself.

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.stat-callout .example}
**Example**

Complement of event $C$ is the set of outcomes in a roll die that are not prime.

*Notation:* $C^c$

*Pronunciation:* C complement

$C^c = \{1, 4, 6\}$
:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-alt: "The die Venn diagram with everything outside circle C shaded crimson. The shaded outcomes are 4, 6, and 1."
die_venn(function(a, b, c) !c, title = "C complement")
```

:::
::::

## Mutually exclusive or disjoint events {.smaller}

**Definition** Mutually exclusive or disjoint events are two events that cannot happen at the same time.

:::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}

::: {.stat-callout .example}
**Examples**

Events A and B are mutually exclusive because an outcome of a roll of a die cannot be even *and* odd.

Events A and C are *not* mutually exclusive because 2 is both an even number and a prime number so event A and C can happen simultaneously.
:::

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-alt: "The die Venn diagram with circle A shaded crimson and circle B shaded navy. The two circles do not touch. The dashed circle C overlaps both."
die_venn(function(a, b, c) a) +
  geom_polygon(data = circle_path(1.1, 0, 0.9), aes(x, y), fill = navy, color = "black", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_path(data = circle_path(0, -0.1, 0.85), aes(x, y), linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = c(0.48, 0.48, 1.6), y = c(0.22, -0.32, 0), label = c("3", "5", "1"),
           size = 10, color = "white")
```

:::
::::

## Events and set notation

<br>

| Description | Notation | Reading | Elements |
|---|---|---|---|
| Union | $A \cup C$ | A or C | $\{2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$ |
| Intersection | $A \cap C$ | A and C | $\{2\}$ |

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Two die Venn diagrams. In the left one, titled A union C, circles A and C are shaded, covering 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6; only 1 is unshaded. In the right one, titled A intersection C, only the overlap of A and C, containing 2, is shaded."
die_venn(function(a, b, c) a | c, title = "A ∪ C") |
  die_venn(function(a, b, c) a & c, title = "A ∩ C")
```

## Set notation

::: {.stat-callout .exercise}
**Exercise**

Use the die Venn diagram to list the outcomes in each event.

a. $A \cup B$
b. $A \cap B$
c. $B \cap C$
d. $B \cup C$
e. $(B \cup C)^c$
f. $A^c \cap C$
:::

## Defining probability

**Frequentist definition**

The probability of an outcome is defined to be the proportion of times the outcome is observed under high number of repetitions of the random process.

##

Assume that we are repeating the random process of a coin flip and are recording $X$, the number of heads in $n$ coin flips. Then

$$P(H) = \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{X}{n}$$

$$P(H) =\frac{1}{2}$$

## Flipping a coin 1,000 times in R

```{r}
#| echo: false
set.seed(8)
```

```{r}
flips <- sample(c("H", "T"), size = 1000, replace = TRUE)
head(flips, 10)
running_prop <- cumsum(flips == "H") / 1:1000
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of the proportion of heads after each of 1,000 simulated coin flips. The proportion jumps around a lot during the first 50 flips, then settles down and stays close to the dashed horizontal line at 0.5."
tibble(flip = 1:1000, prop = running_prop) |>
  ggplot(aes(flip, prop)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = crimson, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(color = navy, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Number of flips, n", y = "X / n") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1))
```

## Defining probability

**Bayesian definition**

When defining probability in addition to considering number of times an outcome occurs, Bayesians consider prior information that they have about an outcome.

More on this in a few weeks!

## Axioms of probability

1) The probability of any event is between zero and one:

. . .

$$0 \leq P(A) \leq 1$$

. . .

2) The probabilities must add up to 1.

. . .

$$P(S) = 1$$

##

3) The probability of mutually exclusive events is additive.

. . .

$$P\left(\bigcup\limits_{i=1}^{\infty} A_{i}\right) = \sum_{i =1}^\infty P(A_i)$$

. . .

::: {.stat-callout .example}
**Example**

For a fair die, each outcome has probability $\frac{1}{6}$. $A$ (even) and $B$ (odd) are mutually exclusive, so

$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) = \frac{3}{6} + \frac{3}{6} = 1$
:::

## Probability of complementary events

$P(A) + P(A^c) = 1$

. . .

::: {.stat-callout .example}
**Example**

If we know the the probability that somebody owns a bike is 0.08, then we would know that the probability that somebody does not own a bike is 0.92.
:::

. . .

::: {.stat-callout .example}
**Example**

$P(C^c) = 1 - P(C) = 1 - \frac{3}{6} = \frac{3}{6}$
:::

## Addition rule

For __any__ two events:

$$P(A \cup C) = P(A) + P(C) - P(A \cap C)$$

:::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}

Why subtract? $A \cap C = \{2\}$ is counted twice: once in $P(A)$ and once in $P(C)$.

$$P(A \cup C) = \frac{3}{6} + \frac{3}{6} - \frac{1}{6} = \frac{5}{6}$$

Check: $A \cup C = \{2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-alt: "The die Venn diagram. Circles A and C are light pink, and their overlap containing 2 is dark crimson, showing the part that would be counted twice."
die_venn(function(a, b, c) a | c, fill = pink, text_col = "black") +
  geom_raster(data = expand_grid(x = seq(-2.4, 2.4, length.out = 400),
                                 y = seq(-1.5, 1.5, length.out = 250)) |>
                filter((x + 1.1)^2 + y^2 <= 0.81, x^2 + (y + 0.1)^2 <= 0.85^2),
              aes(x, y), fill = crimson) +
  geom_path(data = circle_path(-1.1, 0, 0.9), aes(x, y), linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_path(data = circle_path(0, -0.1, 0.85), aes(x, y), linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = -0.5, y = -0.05, label = "2", size = 10, color = "white")
```

:::
::::

## Addition rule

If the events are mutually exclusive, $P(A \cap B) = 0$, and we are back to axiom 3: $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$

. . .

::: {.stat-callout .exercise}
**Exercise**

Roll a fair die. Use the addition rule to find

a. $P(B \cup C)$
b. $P(A \cup B)$
c. $P(\text{at least 5} \cup \text{even})$

Check by listing the outcomes.
:::

## Independence and multiplication rule

Two processes are independent if knowing about the outcome of one does not help predict the outcome of the other.

::: {.stat-callout .example}
**Example**

two flips of a single coin
:::

##

If events A and B are from two independent processes, then

$$P(A \cap B) = P(A) \times P(B)$$

. . .

Probability of getting two heads in two flips of a single coin is

$\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{4}$

. . .

Check with the sample space: $HH$ is 1 of the 4 equally likely outcomes in $\{HH, TT, HT, TH\}$.

## Rolling two dice

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "A 6 by 6 grid of all 36 outcomes of rolling two dice, with the first die on the x-axis and the second die on the y-axis. The single cell where both dice show 6 is crimson."
expand_grid(die1 = 1:6, die2 = 1:6) |>
  mutate(hl = die1 == 6 & die2 == 6) |>
  ggplot(aes(die1, die2, fill = hl)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("(", die1, ",", die2, ")"), color = hl), size = 5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "gray90", `TRUE` = crimson), guide = "none") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "black", `TRUE` = "white"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:6) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:6) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "First die", y = "Second die") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

$P(\text{6 and 6}) = \frac{1}{6} \times \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{36}$

## Independence

::: {.stat-callout .exercise}
**Exercise**

a. You flip a coin and roll a die. What is the probability of heads and a 6?
b. You roll two dice. What is the probability that both are even?
c. You roll a die three times. What is the probability of no 6s at all?
d. You roll a die four times. What is the probability of at least one 6? (Hint: complement!)
:::

# Random variables {.inverse background-color="#A51C30"}

## Random variable

A __random variable__ is a numerical outcome of a random process. We usually write random variables with capital letters.

. . .

::: {.stat-callout .example}
**Example**

Flip a coin twice. Let $X$ be the number of heads.

| Outcome | $HH$ | $HT$ | $TH$ | $TT$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $X$ | 2 | 1 | 1 | 0 |

$X$ can be 0, 1, or 2. Before we flip, we do not know which.
:::

## Random variables are everywhere

A random variable can be...

. . .

- $X$: the height of a randomly selected student

. . .

- $\bar{X}$: the mean height of a random sample of 25 students. Take a different sample, get a different $\bar{X}$!

. . .

- $p$: the proportion of students in a random sample who drink coffee daily

. . .

- $\mu$: the mean height of all students. In Bayesian inference, we treat even a population parameter like $\mu$ as a random variable to describe our uncertainty about it.

. . .

In the coming weeks, we will work with all of these.

## Discrete vs. continuous random variables {.smaller}

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

A __discrete random variable__ takes values we can list (count): 0, 1, 2, ...

::: {.stat-callout .example}
**Examples**

- Number of heads in two flips
- The number on a die
- Number of emails you get tomorrow
:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

A __continuous random variable__ can take any value in an interval. We cannot list them all.

::: {.stat-callout .example}
**Examples**

- Height
- Minutes you wait for the shuttle
- $\bar{X}$, $\mu$
:::

:::
::::

## Discrete or continuous?

::: {.stat-callout .exercise}
**Exercise**

Is each random variable discrete or continuous?

a. Number of courses a randomly selected student takes this semester
b. Time a randomly selected student sleeps tonight
c. Number of 6s in ten rolls of a die
d. GPA of a randomly selected student
e. Proportion of heads in ten flips of a coin
:::

## Probability distribution

The __probability distribution__ of a random variable tells us all its possible values and how probable each one is.

. . .

For a __discrete__ random variable, we can list $P(X = x)$ for every value $x$. These probabilities add up to 1.

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

$X$: number on a fair die

| $x$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $P(X = x)$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ |

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

$X$: number of heads in two flips

| $x$ | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| $P(X = x)$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{2}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ |

:::
::::

## Probability distribution: discrete

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Two bar charts. Left: the number on a fair die, six bars from 1 to 6, each with height one sixth. Right: the number of heads in two coin flips, bars at 0, 1, and 2 with heights one quarter, one half, and one quarter."
die_dist <- tibble(x = 1:6, p = 1/6) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(x), p)) +
  geom_col(fill = crimson, width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = "1/6"), vjust = -0.4, size = 7) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.6)) +
  labs(x = "x: number on a die", y = "P(X = x)")
coin_dist <- tibble(x = 0:2, p = c(1, 2, 1) / 4) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(x), p)) +
  geom_col(fill = navy, width = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = c("1/4", "2/4", "1/4")), vjust = -0.4, size = 7) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.6)) +
  labs(x = "x: number of heads", y = "P(X = x)")
die_dist | coin_dist
```

The heights of the bars are probabilities, and they add up to 1.

## What about a continuous random variable?

$X$: minutes you wait for the shuttle. Any wait between 0 and 10 minutes is equally likely. What is $P(X = 3)$? Exactly 3, not 3.01, not 2.9999...

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Three bar charts of equally likely values between 0 and 10. With 10 possible values, each bar has height 0.1. With 100 possible values, each bar has height 0.01. With 1,000 possible values, the bars are so short, 0.001 each, that they almost disappear."
split_plot <- function(k) {
  tibble(x = seq(0, 10, length.out = k), p = 1 / k) |>
    ggplot(aes(x, p)) +
    geom_col(fill = crimson, width = 10 / k * 0.7) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.11), breaks = c(0, 0.05, 0.1)) +
    labs(x = "minutes", y = "P(X = x)",
         title = paste0(format(k, big.mark = ","), " values: each is 1/", format(k, big.mark = ","))) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 20, hjust = 0.5))
}
split_plot(10) | split_plot(100) | split_plot(1000)
```

More values, smaller probabilities. With infinitely many values, $P(X = 3) = \frac{1}{\infty} = 0$.

## Probability as area under the curve

For a continuous random variable, we cannot talk about $P(X = x)$. Instead, we find the probability that $X$ is in an __interval__. The probability is the __area under the curve__, and the total area under the curve is 1.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "A flat curve at height 0.1 from 0 to 10 minutes, forming a rectangle with total area 1. The region between 2 and 5 minutes is shaded crimson and labeled area = 3 times 0.1 = 0.3."
tibble(x = c(0, 10), y = 0.1) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = 10, ymin = 0, ymax = 0.1, fill = "gray90") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 2, xmax = 5, ymin = 0, ymax = 0.1, fill = crimson) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = 0, y = 0, yend = 0.1), linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 10, xend = 10, y = 0, yend = 0.1), linewidth = 1.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 3.5, y = 0.05, label = "area = 3 × 0.1\n= 0.3", color = "white", size = 7) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:10) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.13), breaks = c(0, 0.1)) +
  labs(x = "X: minutes waiting for the shuttle", y = NULL)
```

$P(2 < X < 5) = 0.3$. And $P(X = 3)$ is the area of a line, which is 0.

## Probability as area under the curve

::: {.stat-callout .exercise}
**Exercise**

The shuttle wait time $X$ is equally likely to be anywhere between 0 and 10 minutes. Draw the picture and find

a. $P(X < 4)$
b. $P(X > 7)$
c. $P(1 < X < 9)$
d. $P(X = 5)$
e. Why is $P(X < 4) = P(X \le 4)$?
:::

## Coming up next class

Next class, the curve will not be flat. It will be bell-shaped: the __normal distribution__.

The idea stays the same: probability = area under the curve.

## Events

Let B represent an event that a randomly selected person in this sample believes in life after death.

. . .

Let C represent an event that a randomly selected person in this sample took a college level science course.

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Venn diagram of the 1,050 people in the GSS sample. Circle B, believes in life after death, and circle C, took a college science course, overlap. The counts are 485 in B only, 375 in both, 75 in C only, and 115 outside both circles."
venn2(counts = c("485", "375", "75", "115"))
```

## Conditional probability

$P(B|C)$ represents a __conditional probability__. So do $P(B^c|C)$, $P(C| B)$ and $P(C|B^c)$. To calculate the probabilities we focus on the row or the column of the given information. We _reduce_ the sample space to this given information.

. . .

Probability that a randomly selected person believes in life after death given that they have taken a college science course
$P(B|C) = \frac{375}{450}$

## Conditional probability

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Two Venn diagrams of the GSS sample. On the left, titled 'All 1,050 people', circles B and C with counts 485, 375, 75, and 115, and the overlap shaded. On the right, titled 'Given C: only the 450 in C', everything outside circle C is grayed out; circle C is light pink with 75, and the overlap with B is crimson with 375."
before <- venn2(function(b, c) b & c, counts = c("485", "375", "75", "115"),
                title = "All 1,050 people")
given_c <- {
  grid <- expand_grid(x = seq(-2.4, 2.4, length.out = 400),
                      y = seq(-1.6, 1.6, length.out = 270)) |>
    mutate(inB = (x + 0.6)^2 + y^2 <= 1,
           inC = (x - 0.6)^2 + y^2 <= 1,
           region = case_when(inB & inC ~ "BC", inC ~ "C", TRUE ~ "out"))
  ggplot() +
    geom_raster(data = grid, aes(x, y, fill = region), show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(BC = crimson, C = pink, out = "gray80")) +
    geom_path(data = circle_path(-0.6), aes(x, y), linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
    geom_path(data = circle_path(0.6), aes(x, y), linewidth = 2) +
    annotate("text", x = -1.55, y = 1.2, label = "B", size = 10, fontface = "bold", color = "gray40") +
    annotate("text", x = 1.55, y = 1.2, label = "C", size = 10, fontface = "bold") +
    annotate("text", x = c(0, 1.1), y = c(0, 0), label = c("375", "75"), size = 8,
             color = c("white", "black")) +
    coord_equal() + theme_void() +
    labs(title = "Given C: only the 450 in C") +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 26))
}
before | given_c
```

$$P(B|C) = \frac{P(B \cap C)}{P(C)} = \frac{375/1050}{450/1050} = \frac{375}{450}$$

## Conditional probability with a die

Roll a fair die. Given that the roll is even, what is the probability that it is prime?

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

Once we know $A$ (even) happened, the sample space shrinks to $\{2, 4, 6\}$. Only 2 is prime.

$$P(C|A) = \frac{P(C \cap A)}{P(A)} = \frac{1/6}{3/6} = \frac{1}{3}$$

Compare: $P(C) = \frac{3}{6}$. Knowing the roll is even changes the probability that it is prime.

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-alt: "The die Venn diagram with everything outside circle A grayed out. Inside A, the overlap with C containing 2 is crimson, and 4 and 6 are on light pink."
die_venn(function(a, b, c) a, fill = pink, text_col = "black") +
  geom_raster(data = expand_grid(x = seq(-2.4, 2.4, length.out = 400),
                                 y = seq(-1.5, 1.5, length.out = 250)) |>
                filter((x + 1.1)^2 + y^2 > 0.81),
              aes(x, y), fill = "gray80") +
  geom_raster(data = expand_grid(x = seq(-2.4, 2.4, length.out = 400),
                                 y = seq(-1.5, 1.5, length.out = 250)) |>
                filter((x + 1.1)^2 + y^2 <= 0.81, x^2 + (y + 0.1)^2 <= 0.85^2),
              aes(x, y), fill = crimson) +
  geom_path(data = circle_path(-1.1, 0, 0.9), aes(x, y), linewidth = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = c(-1.5, -1.5, -0.5), y = c(0.3, -0.3, -0.05), label = c("4", "6", "2"),
           size = 10, color = c("black", "black", "white")) +
  annotate("text", x = -1.75, y = 1.15, label = "A", size = 10, fontface = "bold") +
  labs(title = "Given A: only {2, 4, 6}") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 24))
```

:::
::::

## Conditional probability with a die

::: {.stat-callout .exercise}
**Exercise**

Roll a fair die. Find

a. $P(A|C)$: even, given prime
b. $P(B|C)$: odd, given prime
c. $P(C|B)$: prime, given odd
d. $P(A|B)$: even, given odd
e. $P(\text{6}|A)$ and $P(A|\text{6})$
:::

## Conditional probability

The order matters!

$P(\text{has a dog | like dogs}) \neq$ $P(\text{like dogs | has a dog})$

## Conditional probability

::: {.stat-callout .exercise}
**Exercise**

Using the GSS table, find

a. $P(C|B)$. Is it the same as $P(B|C)$?
b. $P(B^c|C)$
c. $P(C|B^c)$
d. $P(B|C) + P(B^c|C)$. Why do you get this answer?
:::

## Addition rule

$P(B\cup C) = P(B) + P(C) - P(B \cap C)$

. . .

$P(B\cup C) = \frac{860}{1050} + \frac{450}{1050} -\frac{375}{1050} = \frac{935}{1050}$

. . .

$P(B\cup C) = \frac{375}{1050} + \frac{75}{1050} +\frac{485}{1050} = \frac{935}{1050}$

. . .

$P(B\cup C) = 1 - P(B^c \cap C^c) = 1 - \frac{115}{1050} = \frac{935}{1050}$

## Addition rule

::: {.stat-callout .exercise}
**Exercise**

Using the GSS table, find each probability in two ways: with the addition rule, and by adding up cells of the table.

a. $P(B \cup C^c)$
b. $P(B^c \cup C)$
c. $P(B^c \cup C^c)$
:::

## Multiplication rule

Rearranging the definition of conditional probability:

$$P(B \cap C) = P(B|C) \times P(C)$$

. . .

$$P(B \cap C) = \frac{375}{450} \times \frac{450}{1050} = \frac{375}{1050}$$

. . .

If $B$ and $C$ are independent, $P(B|C) = P(B)$ and we are back to $P(B \cap C) = P(B) \times P(C)$.

## Tree diagram

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Tree diagram for the GSS sample. The root splits into 'science course' with probability 0.429 and 'no science course' with probability 0.571. Science course splits into 'believes' with 0.833 and 'does not' with 0.167. No science course splits into 'believes' with 0.808 and 'does not' with 0.192. On the right, the products give the joint probabilities: 0.357, 0.071, 0.462, and 0.110."
r3 <- function(x) format(round(x, 3), nsmall = 3)
pC <- 450 / 1050
pB_C <- 375 / 450
pB_Cc <- 485 / 600
nodes <- tibble(
  x = c(1, 1, 2.3, 2.3, 2.3, 2.3),
  y = c(1.5, -1.5, 2.25, 0.75, -0.75, -2.25),
  label = c("science course", "no science course", "believes", "does not", "believes", "does not")
)
edges <- tibble(
  x = c(0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1), y = c(0, 0, 1.5, 1.5, -1.5, -1.5),
  xend = c(1, 1, 2.3, 2.3, 2.3, 2.3), yend = c(1.5, -1.5, 2.25, 0.75, -0.75, -2.25),
  prob = c(r3(pC), r3(1 - pC), r3(pB_C), r3(1 - pB_C), r3(pB_Cc), r3(1 - pB_Cc))
)
times <- " × "
joint <- tibble(
  x = 2.95, y = c(2.25, 0.75, -0.75, -2.25),
  label = c(paste0(r3(pC), times, r3(pB_C), " = ", r3(pC * pB_C)),
            paste0(r3(pC), times, r3(1 - pB_C), " = ", r3(pC * (1 - pB_C))),
            paste0(r3(1 - pC), times, r3(pB_Cc), " = ", r3((1 - pC) * pB_Cc)),
            paste0(r3(1 - pC), times, r3(1 - pB_Cc), " = ", r3((1 - pC) * (1 - pB_Cc))))
)
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = edges, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
               linewidth = 1.2, color = navy) +
  geom_label(data = edges, aes(x = x + 0.45 * (xend - x), y = y + 0.45 * (yend - y), label = prob),
             size = 6.5, label.size = 0, fill = "#F9F9FB", color = crimson, fontface = "bold") +
  geom_label(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 7,
             fill = "white", label.size = 0.6, label.padding = unit(0.3, "lines")) +
  geom_text(data = joint, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 7, hjust = 0) +
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = 0, size = 5, color = navy) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.1, 4.6)) +
  theme_void()
```

The four joint probabilities are the four cells of the contingency table divided by 1050.

# Practice with contingency tables {.inverse background-color="#A51C30"}

## Hair and eye color

In 1974, 592 statistics students at the University of Delaware reported their hair and eye color. The data are built into R: [HairEyeColor](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/datasets/html/HairEyeColor.html).

```{r}
as.data.frame(HairEyeColor) |>
  count(Hair, Eye, wt = Freq) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Eye, values_from = n)
```

## Hair and eye color

::: {.stat-callout .exercise}
**Exercise**

A student is randomly selected from this sample. Find

a. $P(\text{blue eyes})$
b. $P(\text{blond hair} \cap \text{blue eyes})$
c. $P(\text{blond hair} \cup \text{blue eyes})$
d. $P(\text{blue eyes} | \text{blond hair})$
e. $P(\text{blond hair} | \text{blue eyes})$
f. Are hair color and eye color independent in this sample? Use your answers to (a) and (d).
:::

## College students and their parents

The [drug_use](https://openintrostat.github.io/openintro/reference/drug_use.html) data in the `openintro` package come from a 1979 study of 445 college students and their parents on marijuana use.

```{r}
drug_use |>
  count(student, parents) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = parents, values_from = n)
```

::: {.stat-callout .exercise}
**Exercise**

Find $P(\text{student uses})$, $P(\text{student uses} | \text{parents used})$, and $P(\text{parents used} | \text{student uses})$. Are the student's and the parents' use independent in this sample?
:::

## Brain teaser

::: {.stat-callout .discussion}
**Discussion**

Jordan is a Harvard student. They love data, code in R every night, and took AP Statistics in high school.

Which is more probable?

a. Jordan is a junior.
b. Jordan is a junior *and* concentrates in Statistics.
:::

. . .

__Answer: (a).__ $P(\text{junior} \cap \text{Statistics}) \le P(\text{junior})$. An intersection can never be more probable than either of its events.

## Practice

Draw a Venn diagram of

$(A \cap B)^c \cap (B \cup C)$

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "An empty Venn diagram with three overlapping circles labeled A, B, and C inside a rectangle labeled S."

```

## Practice - answer

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Three Venn diagrams with circles A, B, and C. The first, the complement of A intersection B, shades everything except the overlap of A and B. The second, B union C, shades circles B and C. The third, their intersection, shades circles B and C except the region where A and B overlap."
venn3(function(a, b, c) !(a & b), fill = pink, title = "(A ∩ B)ᶜ") |
  venn3(function(a, b, c) b | c, fill = pink, title = "B ∪ C") |
  venn3(function(a, b, c) !(a & b) & (b | c), title = "(A ∩ B)ᶜ ∩ (B ∪ C)")
```

. . .

Bonus: with our die events ($A$ even, $B$ odd, $C$ prime), which outcomes are in $(A \cap B)^c \cap (B \cup C)$?
